paragraphes: Before you buy locks, you walk around your house. You ask how a burglar could get in.
Maybe through an open window, the garage door, or the roof. You write down each weak point.
Then you choose one protection for each weak point. Experts do this with computer systems, before any attack happens. It is called threat modeling.

decouverte.comme: You think like the burglar and look for a way in. You break nothing. You only think and write.
decouverte.enVrai: A threat is a possible danger for a system. A countermeasure is a protection against a threat. Threat modeling means finding the threats, then choosing the countermeasures.

decouverte.comme: A door can be old and weak. Or a good door can have no lock at all.
decouverte.enVrai: A weak point in a system is called a vulnerability. A security control is a protection, like a lock. A threat can come from a vulnerability or from a missing control.

decouverte.question: When is threat modeling used the most for an application?
options: While the application is being built
Only after an attack
Never, because a strong password is enough
decouverte.answer: While the application is being built
decouverte.explanation: The manual says it is used most often while the application is being built. You can also use it to lower the risk of applications that already run.

decouverte.texte: A team builds an app to order food. Before it writes any code, it asks questions. Who could steal the home addresses? Who could change the price of an order? It writes down each threat. Then it picks a protection for each one.

cards.question: Official definition: “threat modeling”
cards.answer: Threat modeling is a technique by which you can identify potential threats to your systems and applications, as well as identify suitable countermeasures against those threats.
cards.explanation: In simple words: it is a way to find the possible dangers for your systems, and to choose protections against them.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Threat Modeling”. A countermeasure is a protection against a threat. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “threat modeling”?
options: Threat modeling is a technique by which you can identify actual attacks against your systems and applications, as well as identify suitable recovery plans after those attacks.
Threat modeling is a technique by which you can identify potential threats to your systems and applications, as well as measure the money lost from those threats.
Threat modeling is a technique by which you can identify potential threats to your systems and applications, as well as identify suitable countermeasures against those threats.
Threat modeling is a technique by which you can identify potential threats to your networks only, as well as identify suitable countermeasures against those threats.
options_why: It talks about attacks that already happened. Threat modeling looks at potential threats and countermeasures.
The second half is wrong. Threat modeling looks for countermeasures. It does not measure lost money.
It looks close, but the real sentence says systems and applications, not networks only.
cards.answer: Threat modeling is a technique by which you can identify potential threats to your systems and applications, as well as identify suitable countermeasures against those threats.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: threats (the danger) and countermeasures (the protection).

cards.question: Say the official definition of “threat modeling” from memory.
cards.answer: Threat modeling is a technique by which you can identify potential threats to your systems and applications, as well as identify suitable countermeasures against those threats.
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: threats (the danger) and countermeasures (the protection).

cards.question: Official definition: where “threats” can come from
cards.answer: Threats may be related to overall system vulnerabilities or an absence of necessary security controls.
cards.explanation: In simple words: a threat can come from a weak point in the system, or from a protection that is missing.

cards.question: Say, from memory, the official sentence about where “threats” can come from.
cards.answer: Threats may be related to overall system vulnerabilities or an absence of necessary security controls.
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: a weak point in the system, or a missing security control.

cards.question: Official definition: why a threat modeling program is useful
cards.answer: Implementing a structured threat modeling program allows an organization to consistently identify and characterize the threats it faces and then apply appropriate control to the risks associated with those threats.
cards.explanation: In simple words: a regular program gives every project the same habits. Find the threats, describe them, then add the right controls.

cards.question: Say, from memory, the official sentence about why a threat modeling program is useful.
cards.answer: Implementing a structured threat modeling program allows an organization to consistently identify and characterize the threats it faces and then apply appropriate control to the risks associated with those threats.
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: a structured program, threats found in a consistent way, then a fitting control.

cards.question: A team lists what could go wrong with its app before it writes any code. It then picks a protection for each danger. Which technique is this?
options: Threat modeling
A data backup plan
An audit after an incident
A password test
options_why: A backup helps you get data back. It does not find threats in advance.
An audit after an incident comes too late. Here, nothing has happened yet.
A password test checks only one weak point, not all the dangers.
cards.answer: Threat modeling
cards.explanation: Finding the possible threats, then choosing countermeasures: this is the definition.

cards.question: Which sentence BEST describes a countermeasure?
options: A possible danger for a system
A weak point in a system
A report written after an attack
A protection chosen to answer a threat
options_why: This is a threat. A countermeasure is the answer to a threat.
This is a vulnerability. A countermeasure helps to protect it.
A report only records what happened. It does not protect anything by itself.
cards.answer: A protection chosen to answer a threat
cards.explanation: A threat is the danger. A countermeasure is what you do about it.

cards.question: According to the manual, what can a threat be linked to?
options: Only a very skilled hacker
A weak point in the system or a missing security control
Only a mistake by one employee
Only a power cut at the office
options_why: A weak point is enough to create a threat. A skilled hacker is not needed.
A mistake can play a part, but the manual does not say it is the only source.
A power cut is one kind of danger. The manual does not name it as the source.
cards.answer: A weak point in the system or a missing security control
cards.explanation: A weak point that exists, or a protection that is missing, can create a possible threat.

cards.question: A company plans a new app. The team wants to add many protections quickly. What should the team do FIRST?
options: Buy the most expensive security tool
Find the possible threats to the app
Write the user manual for the app
Wait for the first attack and learn from it
options_why: A tool bought too early may protect the wrong places.
A user manual is useful, but it does not help to find threats.
Waiting is reactive. Threat modeling is about acting before an attack.
cards.answer: Find the possible threats to the app
cards.explanation: You need to know the threats before you can choose good protections.

cards.question: When is threat modeling BEST used for a new application?
options: Only after the application is attacked
Only once a year after the launch
Only when the application is removed
While the application is being built
options_why: After an attack is too late. Threat modeling looks ahead.
A yearly check helps, but the manual says it is used most while building.
A removed application no longer needs protection.
cards.answer: While the application is being built
cards.explanation: The manual says it is used most often during development.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a goal of threat modeling?
options: Repairing a system after an attack
Finding possible threats to systems
Choosing suitable countermeasures
Helping to lower the risk of apps already in use
options_why: This is a main goal of threat modeling.
This is a main goal of threat modeling.
The manual says it can also help with existing apps.
cards.answer: Repairing a system after an attack
cards.explanation: Threat modeling looks ahead. Repairing a system after an attack is a different job.

cards.question: A team adds protections without first thinking about the threats. What is the MOST likely result?
options: Every possible attack will be stopped
The protections will work, but cost too much
Some protections may miss the real weak points
The team will need to use a different method
options_why: This is extreme. More protections do not help if they are in the wrong places.
Cost may be a problem, but it is not the main risk here.
Nothing says the method must change. The problem is the missing list of threats.
cards.answer: Some protections may miss the real weak points
cards.explanation: Without a list of threats, protections are chosen by guess. Some real weak points may stay open.

cards.question: An app has run for three years. A manager wants to lower its risk. Which action is BEST?
options: Use threat modeling on the app that is already running
Do nothing, because threat modeling is only for new apps
Shut down the app until it is built again
Wait for users to report problems
options_why: The manual says you can also use it on existing apps.
This is extreme. Threat modeling can help without a shutdown.
Waiting is reactive. Users find problems after the harm is done.
cards.answer: Use threat modeling on the app that is already running
cards.explanation: The manual says threat modeling helps to reduce risk in existing applications and environments.

cards.question: A shop writes: “Someone could steal our customer list.” What is this sentence?
options: A countermeasure, because it is a plan
A vulnerability, because it is a weak point
A threat, because it is a possible danger
A control, because it protects the list
options_why: A countermeasure is a protection. This sentence describes a danger.
A vulnerability is a weak point. This sentence describes a danger, not a weakness.
A control protects. This sentence does not protect anything. It describes a danger.
cards.answer: A threat, because it is a possible danger
cards.explanation: A threat is a possible danger. The shop has not named any protection yet.

cards.question: What does threat modeling do? Say it in your own words.
cards.answer: It finds possible threats to systems and applications. Then it picks countermeasures against them.
cards.explanation: Think of the burglar on paper: first the dangers, then the protections.

cards.question: What is the difference between a threat and a countermeasure?
cards.answer: A threat is a possible danger for a system. A countermeasure is the protection chosen to answer that threat.
cards.explanation: Threat: what could happen. Countermeasure: what you do about it.

cards.question: Name two things that a threat can be linked to.
cards.answer: A weak point in the system, or a missing security control.
cards.explanation: Think of a weak door, or a good door with no lock.

cards.question: When is threat modeling used the most?
cards.answer: Mostly while an application is being built. You can also use it to lower the risk of apps that already run.
cards.explanation: Early is best, but it is never too late.

decouverte.titre: How many doors does your house have?
paragraphes: Your house has a front door, a garage door, and six windows. A burglar has eight places to try.
You close up two windows that nobody uses. Now he has only six places to try.
In computer security, this idea has a name: the attack surface.

decouverte.titre: It is like the doors and windows
decouverte.comme: The more doors and windows a house has, the more places you must watch.
decouverte.enVrai: The attack surface is all the places where an attacker can try to get in. You cannot remove every door, because the system must stay useful. You only remove the doors that have no purpose.

decouverte.question: A server is a computer that gives a service, like a website, to other computers. How can you make its attack surface smaller?
options: Close the services that nobody needs
Add new services for customers
Give every worker access to everything
decouverte.answer: Close the services that nobody needs
decouverte.explanation: Each open service is one more door. Closing the useless ones leaves fewer places to protect. The other two answers add doors.

decouverte.texte: The manual also gives an example from the real world. The attack surface of a building includes how it is built, where it is, and its entrances and exits. An office with ten doors gives an intruder more chances than an office with two.

cards.question: Official definition: “attack surface”
cards.answer: The attack surface is the total range of areas where an attacker can potentially execute a compromise.
cards.explanation: In simple words: all the places where an attacker could try to get in and cause harm.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Threat Modeling”. A compromise means that the attacker succeeds in getting in or doing harm. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “attack surface”?
options: The attack surface is the total range of areas where a defender can potentially detect a compromise.
The attack surface is the total range of areas where an attacker can potentially execute a compromise.
The attack surface is the total number of attackers who can potentially execute a compromise.
The attack surface is the smallest range of areas where an attacker can potentially execute a compromise.
options_why: It mixes up the defender and the attacker. The surface is about where an attacker can act.
The attack surface is about places, not about people.
The real sentence says total range. Smallest changes the meaning.
cards.answer: The attack surface is the total range of areas where an attacker can potentially execute a compromise.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: the total range of areas, an attacker, and a compromise.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “attack surface” from memory.
cards.answer: The attack surface is the total range of areas where an attacker can potentially execute a compromise.
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: the total range of areas, an attacker, and a compromise.

cards.question: Official definition: limiting the “attack surface”
cards.answer: Limiting the attack surface to the minimum number of areas of exposure reduces the opportunities for a threat to become a successful attack.
cards.explanation: In simple words: keep only a few open places, and a threat has fewer chances to become a real attack.

cards.question: Say, from memory, the official sentence about limiting the “attack surface”.
cards.answer: Limiting the attack surface to the minimum number of areas of exposure reduces the opportunities for a threat to become a successful attack.
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: the minimum number of areas, and fewer opportunities for a threat.

cards.question: Official definition: the attack surface of an information system
cards.answer: With an information system, this might include the methods of communication, the access controls, or weaknesses in the underlying architectures.
cards.explanation: In simple words: for a computer system, look at how it communicates, how it controls access, and how it is built.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Threat Modeling”. The architecture is the way the system is built.

cards.question: Say, from memory, the official sentence about the attack surface of an information system.
cards.answer: With an information system, this might include the methods of communication, the access controls, or weaknesses in the underlying architectures.
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: methods of communication, access controls, and weak architecture.

cards.question: Official definition: the attack surface of a physical environment
cards.answer: With a physical environment, the attack surface might include the construction techniques, the location, or the means of entrance and egress.
cards.explanation: In simple words: for a building, look at how it is built, where it is, and where people go in and out.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Threat Modeling”. Egress means exit.

cards.question: Say, from memory, the official sentence about the attack surface of a physical environment.
cards.answer: With a physical environment, the attack surface might include the construction techniques, the location, or the means of entrance and egress.
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: construction techniques, the location, and entrance and egress.

cards.question: Which action makes the attack surface of a server smaller?
options: Opening a new service to the internet
Adding a remote access tool for staff
Connecting the server to one more network
Closing a service that nobody uses
options_why: A new open service is one more door for an attacker.
Remote access adds one more way in, so the surface grows.
Each new connection is one more place to protect.
cards.answer: Closing a service that nobody uses
cards.explanation: Each open service is a door. Fewer doors means fewer chances for an attack.

cards.question: What is the attack surface?
options: The skills and tools of the attacker
The list of protections already in place
The amount of data a company stores
All the places where an attacker can try to get in
options_why: These describe the attacker. The surface describes the places to attack.
Protections are countermeasures. The surface is what they must cover.
Data is something of value. The surface is about the ways to reach it.
cards.answer: All the places where an attacker can try to get in
cards.explanation: Think of all the doors and windows of a house, seen by a burglar.

cards.question: Which item is part of the attack surface of an information system, according to the manual?
options: The yearly budget for security
The methods of communication
The schedule of the nightly backups
The names of the security staff
options_why: Money matters, but a budget is not a place where an attacker can get in.
Backups matter, but the schedule is not a way in for an attacker.
People matter, but a list of names is not a place where an attacker can get in.
cards.answer: The methods of communication
cards.explanation: The manual names the methods of communication, the access controls, and weak architecture.

cards.question: A company opens ten services to the internet but uses only three. What is the BEST way to lower its risk?
options: Buy a second server for the unused services
Rename the unused services to hide them
Close the seven unused services
Ask every user to change their password
options_why: A second server adds more places to protect.
Hiding is not removing. The doors are still there.
This helps, but it does not reduce the number of open doors.
cards.answer: Close the seven unused services
cards.explanation: Each open service is a door. Closing seven of them reduces the chances of an attack.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a way to reduce the attack surface?
options: Adding remote access just in case
Removing features that nobody uses
Turning off services that are not needed
Deleting old accounts that nobody uses
options_why: Fewer features means fewer places to attack.
Fewer open services means fewer doors.
Fewer accounts means fewer ways in.
cards.answer: Adding remote access just in case
cards.explanation: Extra access adds a door. Removing what is not needed closes doors.

cards.question: A manager wants to reduce the attack surface of a system. What should she do FIRST?
options: Close services one at a time until the problem stops
Buy new security tools for every system
Find all the places where an attacker could get in
Write a report for the board of directors
options_why: Closing services at random may break the system and miss the real doors.
Tools bought before you know the doors may be a waste.
A report is useful later. First you must know what to report.
cards.answer: Find all the places where an attacker could get in
cards.explanation: You cannot reduce what you have not found. Look first, then act.
cards.explanation_more: This reasoning is from outside the manual.

cards.question: A manager says: the attack surface and the countermeasures are the same thing. Which answer BEST corrects her?
options: One is a place to attack; the other is a protection
One is a protection; the other is a possible danger
Both words mean a list of the likely attackers
They mean the same thing, but only for buildings
options_why: This is the wrong way round. The attack surface is not a protection.
Neither word means a list of attackers.
They are different ideas, for systems and for buildings.
cards.answer: One is a place to attack; the other is a protection
cards.explanation: The attack surface is what an attacker can reach. Countermeasures are the protections.

cards.question: Why can a company NOT remove the whole attack surface?
options: Attackers will always find another way in anyway
The law says that all services must stay open
Removing it costs too much for every company
The system must stay useful, so some doors stay
options_why: This is extreme. A smaller surface still lowers the risk.
No law says this. The system just needs to do its job.
Cost matters, but the main reason is that the system must stay useful.
cards.answer: The system must stay useful, so some doors stay
cards.explanation: With no door at all, nobody could use the system, not even the people who are allowed in.
cards.explanation_more: The manual talks about the “minimum number of areas of exposure”. The reasoning about use is from outside the manual.

cards.question: A bank adds a new mobile app that connects to its systems. What happens to the attack surface?
options: It stays the same, because the bank is the same
It grows, because there is one more way in
It shrinks, because customers visit fewer branches
It shrinks, because new apps are always safer
options_why: The bank did change. A new app is a new way in.
Fewer visits do not close any digital door.
New does not mean safe. Every new feature is a new door.
cards.answer: It grows, because there is one more way in
cards.explanation: Each new feature that is open to the outside is one more door to protect.

cards.question: Which group lists the areas of a physical attack surface?
options: Communication methods, access controls, and weak architecture
Construction, location, and entrances and exits
Staff, budget, and training plans
Passwords, logs, and encryption keys
options_why: These belong to an information system, not to a building.
These matter, but they are not places where an attacker can get in.
These are protections or tools, not the physical areas of a building.
cards.answer: Construction, location, and entrances and exits
cards.explanation: For a building, look at how it is built, where it is, and where people go in and out.

cards.question: Name two parts of the attack surface of an information system.
cards.answer: For example the methods of communication, the access controls, or weak points in the architecture.
cards.explanation: Each part is a place to watch.

cards.question: Why does a smaller attack surface lower the risk?
cards.answer: Fewer places are open, so a threat has fewer chances to become a real attack.
cards.explanation: A closed door cannot be forced open.

cards.question: What happens to the attack surface when you add a new feature that is open to the outside?
cards.answer: It grows. There is one more door to protect and to watch.
cards.explanation: Each new way in is one more door.

cards.question: Is the location of a building part of its attack surface?
cards.answer: Yes. The manual names the construction, the location, and the entrances and exits.
cards.explanation: Where a building stands changes how easy it is to reach.

paragraphes: A museum has three guards. The first guard thinks about thieves. The second thinks about the most valuable paintings. The third studies the plan of the building, room by room.
None of them is wrong. They just start from different places.
In threat modeling, we call these three ways attacker-centric, asset-centric, and software-centric.

decouverte.titre: The museum and its three guards
decouverte.comme: Guard one studies the possible thieves. Guard two makes a list of valuable objects. Guard three studies the plan and every room.
decouverte.enVrai: Centric means built around something. Attacker-centric means you start from the person who may attack. Asset-centric means you start from what has value. Software-centric means you start from a drawing of the system, part by part.

decouverte.question: You start from a list of the most valuable data of the company. Which approach is this?
options: Asset-centric
Attacker-centric
Software-centric
decouverte.explanation: You start from what has value, so this is the asset-centric approach. The other two start from an attacker profile or from a drawing of the system.

decouverte.texte: Money laundering means making dirty money look clean. A bank studies how launderers work. Then it blocks each step of their method. This is an attacker-centric approach.

cards.question: Official definition: the “attacker-centric” approach
cards.answer: The attacker-centric threat modeling approach starts by identifying the various actors who could potentially cause harm to a system.
cards.explanation: In simple words: you start from the people who could do harm, then you describe what they can do.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Threat Modeling”. The manual adds that you profile their skills and their motives. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of the “attacker-centric” approach?
options: The attacker-centric threat modeling approach starts by identifying the most valuable assets that an attacker could potentially steal from a system.
The attacker-centric threat modeling approach starts by drawing the various components that could potentially cause harm to a system.
The attacker-centric threat modeling approach starts by identifying the one actor who is most likely to cause harm to a system.
The attacker-centric threat modeling approach starts by identifying the various actors who could potentially cause harm to a system.
options_why: This is the idea of the asset-centric approach. It starts from what has value.
This is the idea of the software-centric approach. It starts from a drawing.
The real sentence says various actors, not one actor.
cards.answer: The attacker-centric threat modeling approach starts by identifying the various actors who could potentially cause harm to a system.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: the various actors who could cause harm to a system.

cards.question: Say, from memory, the official definition of the “attacker-centric” approach.
cards.answer: The attacker-centric threat modeling approach starts by identifying the various actors who could potentially cause harm to a system.
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: the various actors who could cause harm to a system.

cards.question: Official definition: the “asset-centric” approach
cards.answer: As opposed to an attacker-centric approach, an asset-centric threat model identifies the assets of value first.
cards.explanation: In simple words: you start from what matters most, then you ask how an attacker could take it.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Threat Modeling”. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of the “asset-centric” approach?
options: As opposed to an attacker-centric approach, an asset-centric threat model identifies the assets of value first.
As opposed to an attacker-centric approach, an asset-centric threat model identifies the attackers of value first.
As opposed to an attacker-centric approach, an asset-centric threat model identifies the assets of value last.
As opposed to a software-centric approach, an asset-centric threat model identifies the assets of value first.
options_why: An asset-centric model starts from assets, not from attackers.
The key word is first. The assets of value come before anything else.
The real sentence compares the approach with the attacker-centric one.
cards.answer: As opposed to an attacker-centric approach, an asset-centric threat model identifies the assets of value first.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: the assets of value come first.

cards.question: Say, from memory, the official definition of the “asset-centric” approach.
cards.answer: As opposed to an attacker-centric approach, an asset-centric threat model identifies the assets of value first.
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: the assets of value come first.

cards.question: Official definition: the “software-centric” approach
cards.answer: In this approach, the system is represented as a set of interconnected processes, using architecture diagrams such as dataflow diagrams (DFDs) or component diagrams.
cards.explanation: In simple words: you draw the system as linked parts, then you look for threats on each part.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Threat Modeling”. The manual also calls it the system-centric approach. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of the “software-centric” approach?
options: In this approach, the system is represented as a set of valuable assets, using lists such as asset registers or inventory sheets.
In this approach, the system is represented as a set of interconnected processes, using attacker profiles such as skill lists or motive charts.
In this approach, the system is represented as a set of interconnected processes, using architecture diagrams such as dataflow diagrams (DFDs) or component diagrams.
In this approach, the system is represented as a set of independent processes, using architecture diagrams such as dataflow diagrams (DFDs) or component diagrams.
options_why: This is the asset-centric idea. The software-centric approach uses diagrams.
Attacker profiles belong to the attacker-centric approach. This approach uses diagrams.
The real sentence says interconnected, not independent. The parts are linked.
cards.answer: In this approach, the system is represented as a set of interconnected processes, using architecture diagrams such as dataflow diagrams (DFDs) or component diagrams.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: interconnected processes, shown with architecture diagrams like DFDs.

cards.question: Say, from memory, the official definition of the “software-centric” approach.
cards.answer: In this approach, the system is represented as a set of interconnected processes, using architecture diagrams such as dataflow diagrams (DFDs) or component diagrams.
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: interconnected processes, shown with architecture diagrams like DFDs.

cards.question: A team draws its application as linked parts. It looks for a possible attack on each part. Which approach is this?
options: Software-centric (or system-centric)
Attacker-centric
Asset-centric
None, because a drawing is not part of threat modeling
options_why: It does not start from a profile of attackers. It starts from the drawing.
It does not start from a list of valuable data. It starts from the parts.
Drawings are exactly how this approach works.
cards.answer: Software-centric (or system-centric)
cards.explanation: A drawing of linked parts is the starting point of the software-centric approach.

cards.question: What does the attacker-centric approach start from?
options: A list of the most valuable assets
A drawing of the parts of the system
A profile of the people who could cause harm
A list of the laws that apply to the company
options_why: This is the starting point of the asset-centric approach.
This is the starting point of the software-centric approach.
Laws matter, but they are not the starting point of this approach.
cards.answer: A profile of the people who could cause harm
cards.explanation: You profile the skills and motives of possible attackers, then keep the most likely ones.

cards.question: Which sentence describes the asset-centric approach?
options: You start from the likely attackers, then study what they want
You start from what has value, then study how to protect it
You start from a drawing, then study each part of it
You start from the laws, then study the attackers
options_why: This is the attacker-centric approach.
This is the software-centric approach.
The approach does not start from laws or attackers.
cards.answer: You start from what has value, then study how to protect it
cards.explanation: The assets of value come first. Then you study how an attacker might harm them.

cards.question: A hospital must show an auditor that patient data is well protected. Which approach is BEST?
options: Attacker-centric
Software-centric
None, because audits do not use threat models
Asset-centric
options_why: Rules usually name the data to protect. This approach starts from attackers.
This approach starts from a drawing of the system, not from the protected data.
The manual says the asset-centric approach helps to check compliance.
cards.answer: Asset-centric
cards.explanation: Many rules protect one type of data, like health data. Starting from the asset follows those rules.

cards.question: A military team wants to plan against a known enemy. Which approach is BEST?
options: Asset-centric
Software-centric
Any approach, because they are all the same
Attacker-centric
options_why: The team studies the enemy first, not the valuable objects.
The team needs to study the enemy, not a drawing of a system.
The manual links military planning to the attacker-centric approach.
cards.answer: Attacker-centric
cards.explanation: The manual says tactical military intelligence is usually driven by an attacker-centric model.

cards.question: Which task is MOST typical of the attacker-centric approach?
options: Drawing a data flow diagram of the application
Describing the motives of a likely hacker
Ranking data by its value to the company
Checking that stored data follows the law
options_why: This is a software-centric task.
This is an asset-centric task.
This is closer to the asset-centric approach.
cards.answer: Describing the motives of a likely hacker
cards.explanation: You profile the skills and motives of a possible attacker.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a software-centric task?
options: Drawing the system with a data flow diagram
Looking for attacks against each part of the diagram
Profiling the skills of a possible attacker
Checking if a control exists for each component
options_why: This is a main step of the software-centric approach.
Analysts do this with the diagram.
The manual says analysts check this for each component.
cards.answer: Profiling the skills of a possible attacker
cards.explanation: Profiling an attacker belongs to the attacker-centric approach.

cards.question: A team will use the asset-centric approach. What should it do FIRST?
options: Identify the assets of value
Profile the likely attackers
Draw a diagram of every component
Measure the damage from an attack
options_why: This comes from the attacker-centric approach.
This comes from the software-centric approach.
You can only measure damage after you know the assets.
cards.answer: Identify the assets of value
cards.explanation: The key word of the definition is first: the assets of value come before anything else.

cards.question: A bank wants to stop money laundering. It studies how launderers work and blocks each step. Which approach is it using?
options: Asset-centric
Software-centric
Attacker-centric
None, because this is not threat modeling
options_why: It does not start from valuable data. It starts from the people who attack.
It does not start from a drawing of the system.
The manual gives this as an example of the attacker-centric approach.
cards.answer: Attacker-centric
cards.explanation: The bank studies how the attackers act, so it follows an attacker-centric model.

cards.question: Why do different organizations choose different approaches?
options: Their rules, methods, and systems prefer different ones
Only one approach is correct and the others are old
The exam accepts only one of the three approaches
Small companies must always use the attacker-centric one
options_why: All three are valid. A CISSP must be able to use all three.
The manual says a CISSP should be able to apply all three.
The manual has no such rule.
cards.answer: Their rules, methods, and systems prefer different ones
cards.explanation: Different risk methods, compliance rules, and systems prefer one approach or another.

cards.question: Why does the attacker-centric approach help when there are too many scenarios?
cards.answer: You keep only the most likely attackers. So you study fewer scenarios.
cards.explanation: You study realistic threats, not every threat you can imagine.

cards.question: Why does the asset-centric approach help to show compliance?
cards.answer: Many rules protect one type of data, like health data or card data. Starting from the asset follows those rules.
cards.explanation: The rule names the asset to protect, so you start from the same point.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Threat Modeling”. Examples: PHI under HIPAA, PII under the GDPR, cardholder data under PCI-DSS.

cards.question: What does DFD stand for, and what is it used for?
cards.answer: Data flow diagram. It shows how data moves between the parts of a system.
cards.explanation: Each arrow on the diagram is a place where a threat can appear.
cards.explanation_more: The manual gives the DFD as an example of an architecture diagram. The explanation of the diagram is from outside the manual.

cards.question: Name two fields that often use the attacker-centric approach.
cards.answer: Tactical military intelligence, and the fight against money laundering (AML).
cards.explanation: In both cases, you study what the opponent does so that you can stop it.

paragraphes: One morning, your game account has a new username and a changed score. Later, the person who did it says he never touched your account.
Three things happened. He pretended to be you. He changed your data. He denied what he did.
Microsoft experts sort threats like these with a memory trick called STRIDE.

decouverte.comme: To remember a shopping list, you keep one word made from the first letter of each item.
decouverte.enVrai: STRIDE is a mnemonic: a memory trick made of first letters. Each letter is one type of threat: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.

decouverte.titre: The first three letters at school
decouverte.comme: One student copies a parent's signature on a note. Another student erases a grade on a report card. A third says “it was not me”, and nobody saw.
decouverte.enVrai: Copying an identity is spoofing. Changing data is tampering. Denying that you did something is repudiation.

decouverte.question: Someone changes the number of items in an online order before it is saved. Which STRIDE threat is this?
options: Spoofing (faking an identity)
Tampering (changing data)
Repudiation (denying an action)
decouverte.explanation: Nothing is false about the person's identity. The data is what gets changed. The other two answers are about identity and denial.

decouverte.texte: Spammers send unwanted emails in large numbers. They change the “From:” field of an email. The name shown is the name of someone you trust. This is a common example of spoofing.

cards.question: Official definition: “STRIDE”
cards.answer: STRIDE is a threat modeling methodology developed by Microsoft in the late 1990s to help identify and classify computer security threats.
cards.explanation: In simple words: STRIDE is a method from Microsoft. It helps you find threats and put them in groups.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “STRIDE” from memory.
cards.answer: STRIDE is a threat modeling methodology developed by Microsoft in the late 1990s to help identify and classify computer security threats.
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: Microsoft, the late 1990s, and identify and classify.

cards.question: Official definition: the name “STRIDE”
cards.answer: The name itself is a mnemonic for six categories of security threats, discussed here:
cards.explanation: In simple words: each letter of the name stands for one of six types of threat.

cards.question: Say, from memory, the official sentence about the name “STRIDE”.
cards.answer: The name itself is a mnemonic for six categories of security threats, discussed here:
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: a mnemonic, six categories, and security threats.

cards.question: Official definition: “spoofing” (the S of STRIDE)
cards.answer: Spoofing is an attack during which a malicious party assumes the identity of another party (either a user or a system) by falsifying information.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the attacker pretends to be someone else, or another system, by using false information.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Threat Modeling”. The manual gives two examples: a changed “From:” field in an email, and stolen sign-in details that are used. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “spoofing”?
options: Spoofing is an attack during which a malicious party assumes the identity of another party (only a human user) by falsifying information.
Spoofing is an attack during which a malicious party changes the data of another party (either a user or a system) by falsifying information.
Spoofing is an attack during which a trusted party assumes the identity of another party (either a user or a system) by falsifying information.
Spoofing is an attack during which a malicious party assumes the identity of another party (either a user or a system) by falsifying information.
options_why: The real sentence says either a user or a system. A system can be faked too.
Changing data is tampering. Spoofing is about taking an identity.
The attacker is a malicious party, not a trusted one.
cards.answer: Spoofing is an attack during which a malicious party assumes the identity of another party (either a user or a system) by falsifying information.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: a malicious party, the identity of another party, and falsifying information.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “spoofing” from memory.
cards.answer: Spoofing is an attack during which a malicious party assumes the identity of another party (either a user or a system) by falsifying information.
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: a malicious party, the identity of another party, and falsifying information.

cards.question: Official definition: “data tampering” (the T of STRIDE)
cards.answer: Data tampering is an attack on the integrity of data by intentionally and maliciously manipulating data.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the attacker changes data on purpose. The data is no longer correct.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Threat Modeling”. The manual says data can be changed on a disk, in memory, or on the network. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “data tampering”?
options: Data tampering is an attack on the availability of data by intentionally and maliciously manipulating data.
Data tampering is an attack on the integrity of data by intentionally and maliciously manipulating data.
Data tampering is an attack on the confidentiality of data by intentionally and maliciously copying data.
Data tampering is an attack on the integrity of data by accidentally and carelessly manipulating data.
options_why: Tampering hits integrity. Availability is about reaching the data.
Copying data is about secrecy. Tampering changes data and hits integrity.
Tampering is on purpose, with bad intent. It is not an accident.
cards.answer: Data tampering is an attack on the integrity of data by intentionally and maliciously manipulating data.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: an attack on integrity, done intentionally and maliciously.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “data tampering” from memory.
cards.answer: Data tampering is an attack on the integrity of data by intentionally and maliciously manipulating data.
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: an attack on integrity, done intentionally and maliciously.

cards.question: Official definition: “repudiation” (the R of STRIDE)
cards.answer: Repudiation is the ability of a party to deny that they are responsible for performing an action.
cards.explanation: In simple words: someone says “it was not me”, and nobody can prove the opposite.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Threat Modeling”. The manual gives a signature on a mail delivery as an example of non-repudiation. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “repudiation”?
options: Repudiation is the ability of a party to prove that they are responsible for performing an action.
Repudiation is the ability of a party to deny that they are responsible for performing an action.
Repudiation is the ability of a party to deny that they have access to a system.
Repudiation is the ability of a system to deny that a party is responsible for performing an action.
options_why: This is the opposite. Repudiation is about denying, not proving.
Repudiation is about denying an action, not about access.
It is the party who denies, not the system.
cards.answer: Repudiation is the ability of a party to deny that they are responsible for performing an action.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: a party that can deny responsibility for an action.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “repudiation” from memory.
cards.answer: Repudiation is the ability of a party to deny that they are responsible for performing an action.
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: a party that can deny responsibility for an action.

cards.question: A customer orders shoes, then says he never ordered them. The shop has no proof. Which STRIDE threat is this?
options: Spoofing
Tampering
Denial of service
Repudiation
options_why: Spoofing is a false identity. Here the customer denies an action.
Tampering is changed data. Here nobody changed the order.
A denial of service blocks access to a site. That did not happen here.
cards.answer: Repudiation
cards.explanation: Denying an action when nobody can prove the opposite is repudiation.

cards.question: A person changes the “From:” field of an email to look like your boss. Which STRIDE threat is this?
options: Spoofing
Tampering
Repudiation
Information disclosure
options_why: The text of the email is not the target. The identity of the sender is.
Nobody is denying an action here.
No secret was shown to the wrong person.
cards.answer: Spoofing
cards.explanation: The attacker pretends to be someone else. This is the manual's own example of spoofing.

cards.question: A hacker changes a salary value on a server's disk. Which STRIDE threat is this?
options: Spoofing
Repudiation
Tampering
Elevation of privilege
options_why: The hacker does not pretend to be someone. He changes data.
Nobody denies an action here.
Nothing says the hacker raised his rights. The data was changed.
cards.answer: Tampering
cards.explanation: Changing data on purpose is tampering. The manual says it can happen on disk, in memory, or on the network.

cards.question: Which control BEST helps to prevent repudiation in an app?
options: Logs and digital signatures for risky actions
Strong encryption for all of the stored files and backups
Extra servers that start when the first one fails
Checks on everything that users type into forms
options_why: Encryption protects secrecy. It does not prove who did an action.
Extra servers help availability, not proof of actions.
These checks help against tampering.
cards.answer: Logs and digital signatures for risky actions
cards.explanation: Logs and signatures leave proof of who did what.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Threat Modeling”: complete logging, digital signatures, and multifactor authentication.

cards.question: A hacker signs in with an employee's stolen password. Which STRIDE threat is MOST likely?
options: Tampering
Repudiation
Spoofing
Elevation of privilege
options_why: The hacker did not change any data. He pretended to be the employee.
Nobody denied an action here.
He took the employee's identity. Raising his own rights is a different threat.
cards.answer: Spoofing
cards.explanation: Using stolen sign-in details to act as someone else is spoofing.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT an example of spoofing?
options: A hacker signs in with a stolen password
A customer says he never bought an item
A spammer changes the “From:” field of an email
An attacker pretends to be a trusted system
options_why: He pretends to be the real user.
The sender is false, so this is spoofing.
A false system identity is spoofing too.
cards.answer: A customer says he never bought an item
cards.explanation: Denying an action is repudiation, not spoofing.

cards.question: Which security goal does data tampering attack?
options: Confidentiality
Availability
Non-repudiation
Integrity
options_why: Confidentiality is about who can see data. Tampering changes data.
Availability is about reaching data. Tampering changes data.
Non-repudiation is about proof of actions.
cards.answer: Integrity
cards.explanation: Integrity means that data stays correct. Tampering makes it wrong on purpose.

cards.question: What is the difference between spoofing and tampering?
options: Spoofing changes data, and tampering fakes an identity
Spoofing is on purpose, but tampering is by accident
Spoofing hits availability; tampering hits confidentiality
Spoofing fakes an identity; tampering changes data
options_why: The two answers are the wrong way round.
Both are attacks that are done on purpose.
Neither goal is the one that these threats hit.
cards.answer: Spoofing fakes an identity; tampering changes data
cards.explanation: Spoofing is about who you pretend to be. Tampering is about what you change.

cards.question: A manager learns that an app accepts any text that users type. What should she ask the team to do FIRST?
options: Remove the app from the internet right now
Review how the app checks user input
Add more servers for the traffic
Tell users to type more carefully
options_why: This is extreme. First check how big the risk is.
More servers do not fix unchecked input.
Users cannot be the only protection. The app must check input.
cards.answer: Review how the app checks user input
cards.explanation: Evaluate first, then act. Unchecked input can allow tampering.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Threat Modeling”: apps that do not properly validate user input.

cards.question: In STRIDE, which threat comes right AFTER Tampering?
options: Spoofing
Information disclosure
Repudiation
Denial of service
options_why: Spoofing is the first letter, S. It comes before Tampering.
Information disclosure is the fourth letter, I.
Denial of service is the fifth letter, D.
cards.answer: Repudiation
cards.explanation: The order is S, T, R, I, D, E. After T comes R.

cards.question: What does the S in STRIDE stand for?
cards.answer: Spoofing. The attacker pretends to be another person or system by using false information.
cards.explanation: Think of a mask.

cards.question: What does the T in STRIDE stand for?
cards.answer: Tampering. The attacker changes data on purpose.
cards.explanation: It attacks integrity.

cards.question: What does the R in STRIDE stand for?
cards.answer: Repudiation. Someone denies an action, and nobody can prove the opposite.
cards.explanation: Think: “it was not me”.

cards.question: Which protections help to stop repudiation in an app?
cards.answer: Complete logging, digital signatures, and multi-factor authentication, mostly for high-risk actions.
cards.explanation: Each one leaves proof of who did what.

decouverte.titre: The diary, the canteen, and the keys
paragraphes: A classmate reads your diary without asking. Ten students block the canteen door, so nobody else can get in. Another student finds the keys of the principal.
Three situations, three more STRIDE threats. They complete S, T, and R with I, D, and E.

decouverte.comme: Ten students stand in front of the canteen door. The other students have the right to go in, but they cannot get through.
decouverte.enVrai: This is a denial of service: legitimate users cannot reach a resource. Legitimate means allowed. This threat attacks availability.

decouverte.comme: An ordinary student gets the keys of the principal. He can open every door in the school.
decouverte.enVrai: This is elevation of privilege: a user with no special rights gets the rights of an administrator. An administrator is a user who can control the whole system. The manual calls this “the keys to the kingdom”.

decouverte.question: An ordinary employee finds a way to open the admin page of the website. Which STRIDE threat is this?
options: Elevation of privilege
Information disclosure
Denial of service
decouverte.explanation: He goes from ordinary user to administrator, so his rights go up. No data leaked and no service is blocked.

decouverte.texte: An employee sends the salary list to the wrong person. No hacker is involved. But the information went to someone who had no right to see it. This is information disclosure.

cards.question: Official definition: “information disclosure” (the I of STRIDE)
cards.answer: Information disclosure is when information is shared with an unauthorized party — such as during a data breach or when inadvertently sending an email to the wrong person.
cards.explanation: In simple words: someone sees information that they should not see. It hits confidentiality.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Threat Modeling”. Inadvertently means by mistake. The manual names data encryption and strong access control as protections. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “information disclosure”?
options: Information disclosure is when information is shared with an unauthorized party — such as during a data breach or when inadvertently sending an email to the wrong person.
Information disclosure is when information is changed by an unauthorized party — such as during a data breach or when inadvertently sending an email to the wrong person.
Information disclosure is when information is shared with an authorized party — such as during a data breach or when inadvertently sending an email to the wrong person.
Information disclosure is when information is shared with an unauthorized party only during a data breach, and never by mistake.
options_why: Changing information is tampering. Disclosure is about sharing it with the wrong party.
The key word is unauthorized. Sharing with an authorized party is not a threat.
This is too narrow. The real sentence also includes sending an email to the wrong person.
cards.answer: Information disclosure is when information is shared with an unauthorized party — such as during a data breach or when inadvertently sending an email to the wrong person.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: shared with an unauthorized party, even by mistake.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “information disclosure” from memory.
cards.answer: Information disclosure is when information is shared with an unauthorized party — such as during a data breach or when inadvertently sending an email to the wrong person.
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: shared with an unauthorized party, even by mistake.

cards.question: Official definition: “denial-of-service attack” (the D of STRIDE)
cards.answer: A denial-of-service (DoS) attack is a common availability attack that denies access to resources by legitimate users.
cards.explanation: In simple words: people who have the right to use the system can no longer use it. Availability falls.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Threat Modeling”. The manual advises you to watch for unusually high use of resources by one user. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “denial-of-service attack”?
options: A denial-of-service (DoS) attack is a common confidentiality attack that denies access to resources by legitimate users.
A denial-of-service (DoS) attack is a common availability attack that gives access to resources to unauthorized users.
A denial-of-service (DoS) attack is a common availability attack that denies access to resources by legitimate users.
A denial-of-service (DoS) attack is a common integrity attack that changes resources used by legitimate users.
options_why: A DoS attack hits availability. Confidentiality is about who can see data.
A DoS attack denies access to legitimate users. It does not give access to others.
A DoS attack blocks access. It does not change data, so it is not an integrity attack.
cards.answer: A denial-of-service (DoS) attack is a common availability attack that denies access to resources by legitimate users.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: a common availability attack that denies access to legitimate users.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “denial-of-service attack” from memory.
cards.answer: A denial-of-service (DoS) attack is a common availability attack that denies access to resources by legitimate users.
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: a common availability attack that denies access to legitimate users.

cards.question: Official definition: “elevation of privilege” (the E of STRIDE)
cards.answer: Elevation of privilege (or privilege escalation) occurs when an unprivileged user is able to upgrade their privileges to those of a privileged user (e.g., a system administrator).
cards.explanation: In simple words: an ordinary user becomes an administrator. He goes up one level of rights.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Threat Modeling”. The manual advises you to check identity again before any privileged access, and to use multifactor authentication. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “elevation of privilege”?
options: Elevation of privilege (or privilege escalation) occurs when an unprivileged user is able to upgrade their privileges to those of a privileged user (e.g., a system administrator).
Elevation of privilege (or privilege escalation) occurs when a privileged user is able to downgrade their privileges to those of an unprivileged user (e.g., a guest account).
Elevation of privilege (or privilege escalation) occurs when an unprivileged user is able to copy the identity of a privileged user (e.g., a system administrator).
Elevation of privilege (or privilege escalation) occurs when an unprivileged user is given temporary privileges by a system administrator (e.g., for a help desk task).
options_why: This is the wrong way round. The privileges go up, not down.
Copying an identity is spoofing. Elevation of privilege is about upgrading the user's own rights.
This is allowed access. The threat is when the user raises his rights without permission.
cards.answer: Elevation of privilege (or privilege escalation) occurs when an unprivileged user is able to upgrade their privileges to those of a privileged user (e.g., a system administrator).
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: an unprivileged user upgrades to the privileges of a privileged user.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “elevation of privilege” from memory.
cards.answer: Elevation of privilege (or privilege escalation) occurs when an unprivileged user is able to upgrade their privileges to those of a privileged user (e.g., a system administrator).
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: an unprivileged user upgrades to the privileges of a privileged user.

cards.question: An email with customer data goes to the wrong person by mistake. Which STRIDE threat is this?
options: Tampering
Repudiation
Elevation of privilege
Information disclosure
options_why: Nothing was changed. Someone saw data that they should not see.
Nobody denies an action here.
Nobody got higher rights. The data went to the wrong person.
cards.answer: Information disclosure
cards.explanation: The data was shared with a party that has no right to it. This is information disclosure.

cards.question: One user sends millions of requests, and the site is slow for everyone. Which STRIDE threat is this?
options: Information disclosure
Denial of service
Spoofing
Elevation of privilege
options_why: No secret was shown to anyone.
Nobody pretended to be another person.
Nobody got higher rights. The site is simply too busy.
cards.answer: Denial of service
cards.explanation: Legitimate users cannot use the site well. This is a loss of availability.

cards.question: An ordinary user gets the rights of a system administrator. Which STRIDE threat is this?
options: Spoofing
Elevation of privilege
Tampering
Information disclosure
options_why: The user does not pretend to be someone else. His own rights go up.
The question is about rights, not about changed data.
No data was shown to the wrong person in this example.
cards.answer: Elevation of privilege
cards.explanation: An unprivileged user upgrades to the privileges of a privileged user.

cards.question: Which control BEST protects against information disclosure?
options: Complete logs of every action that users take
Extra servers that start when the main one fails
Checks on everything that users type into forms
Data encryption and strong access control
options_why: Logs help against repudiation, not against disclosure.
Extra servers help availability.
Input checks help against tampering.
cards.answer: Data encryption and strong access control
cards.explanation: Encryption and strong access control keep unauthorized parties from reading the data.

cards.question: A manager wants to lower the risk of elevation of privilege. Which action is BEST?
options: Check identity again before giving privileged access
Give every user admin rights, to avoid slow help desk calls
Encrypt all of the log files of the application
Add more network speed for busy hours
options_why: This gives everyone the keys. It makes the risk much bigger.
Encryption protects secrecy. It does not stop a user from raising his rights.
Speed does not control who gets rights.
cards.answer: Check identity again before giving privileged access
cards.explanation: The manual says systems should check identity and credentials again before privileged access.

cards.question: Which control would MOST help to spot a possible denial of service?
options: Encrypting all of the data when it is stored on disk
Asking users to sign each action with a digital signature
Watching for unusually high use of resources by one user
Giving every user a stronger password for sign-in
options_why: Encryption protects secrecy, not availability.
Signatures give proof of actions. They do not show an overload.
Strong passwords do not show an overload.
cards.answer: Watching for unusually high use of resources by one user
cards.explanation: Very high use by one user may be a sign of abuse, on purpose or by mistake.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT an example of information disclosure?
options: A user changes the price of an order
A data breach reveals medical records
An employee sends a salary list to the wrong person
A stolen laptop shows customer files to a stranger
options_why: Medical records are shown to people who should not see them.
Data goes to the wrong person, so this is disclosure.
A stranger can see private data, so this is disclosure.
cards.answer: A user changes the price of an order
cards.explanation: Changing a price is tampering, not disclosure.

cards.question: Which security goal does a denial-of-service attack hit?
options: Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
Non-repudiation
options_why: Confidentiality is about who can see data.
Integrity is about keeping data correct.
Non-repudiation is about proof of actions.
cards.answer: Availability
cards.explanation: Legitimate users cannot reach the resource. That is a loss of availability.

cards.question: One account uses far more resources than all the others. What should the security manager do FIRST?
options: Block the account forever and delete all of its data
Check if the activity is abuse or a mistake
Buy a bigger server for the busy account
Ignore it, because it is only one account
options_why: This is extreme. The use may be a mistake, not an attack.
This ignores the cause and only treats the symptom.
One account can use up the resources of a whole system.
cards.answer: Check if the activity is abuse or a mistake
cards.explanation: Evaluate before you act. The manual says high use may be on purpose or not.

cards.question: How is information disclosure different from tampering?
options: Disclosure changes data for others, and tampering shows data
They are the same, because both involve data
Disclosure hits availability; tampering hits confidentiality
Disclosure shows data to others; tampering changes data
options_why: The two answers are the wrong way round.
They hit different goals: confidentiality and integrity.
Neither goal is the one that these threats hit.
cards.answer: Disclosure shows data to others; tampering changes data
cards.explanation: Disclosure hits confidentiality. Tampering hits integrity.

cards.question: Which STRIDE threat attacks confidentiality?
cards.answer: Information disclosure. Information is shared with an unauthorized party.
cards.explanation: Think of the diary that someone reads.

cards.question: Which STRIDE threat attacks availability?
cards.answer: Denial of service. Legitimate users cannot reach a resource.
cards.explanation: Think of the blocked canteen door.

cards.question: What should a system do before it gives privileged access?
cards.answer: Check the user's identity and credentials again, and use multi-factor authentication when possible.
cards.explanation: This is the defense against elevation of privilege.

cards.question: What does “the keys to the kingdom” mean in STRIDE?
cards.answer: Elevation of privilege can give an attacker access to, and control over, sensitive data and systems.
cards.explanation: The higher the rights, the bigger the damage.

concepts.name: PASTA: simulating the attack in seven steps

paragraphes: A fire station plans a drill. First it decides what it must save. Then it marks the limits of the building and splits it into rooms.
Next it looks for dangers and weak points. It writes down what could happen. At the end, it counts the damage.
PASTA follows almost the same path for computer attacks.

decouverte.comme: The director talks about goals and money. The technicians talk about servers and weak points. A good translator links the two.
decouverte.enVrai: PASTA starts from the goals of the business, then goes down to the technical side. So management can understand the result. The picture stops here: PASTA does not translate words. It links two ways of thinking.

decouverte.question: What is the first step of PASTA?
options: Define objectives
Vulnerability analysis
Attack enumeration
decouverte.explanation: PASTA starts with the goals of the business, before the technical side. The other two steps come later.

decouverte.texte: Objective: never lose a payment. Technical scope: the website, the customer list, and the payment service. Then the team splits the app into parts and looks for threats, weak points, and attacks. It ends by measuring the risk and the damage.

cards.question: Official definition: “PASTA”
cards.answer: The Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis (PASTA) is a risk-based threat model, developed in 2012, that supports dynamic threat analysis.
cards.explanation: In simple words: PASTA is a model based on risk. It was made in 2012 and it can follow changes in the threats.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Threat Modeling”. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

options: The Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis (PASTA) is a risk-based threat model, developed in the late 1990s, that supports dynamic threat analysis.
The Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis (PASTA) is a data-based threat model, developed in 2012, that supports dynamic threat analysis.
The Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis (PASTA) is a risk-based threat model, developed in 2012, that supports static threat analysis.
The Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis (PASTA) is a risk-based threat model, developed in 2012, that supports dynamic threat analysis.
options_why: The late 1990s is the time of STRIDE. PASTA was developed in 2012.
PASTA is risk-based. Data-based is not the word of the definition.
The real sentence says dynamic, not static.
cards.answer: The Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis (PASTA) is a risk-based threat model, developed in 2012, that supports dynamic threat analysis.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: risk-based, developed in 2012, and dynamic.

cards.question: Official definition: what makes “PASTA” useful for management
cards.answer: The PASTA methodology integrates business objectives with technical requirements, making the output more easily understood by upper management.
cards.explanation: In simple words: PASTA links the goals of the business with the technical side, so management can follow the result.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Threat Modeling”. You will need to know this sentence word for word.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official one about what makes “PASTA” useful for management?
options: The PASTA methodology separates business objectives from technical requirements, making the output more easily understood by upper management.
The PASTA methodology integrates business objectives with technical requirements, making the output more easily understood by upper management.
The PASTA methodology integrates business objectives with technical requirements, making the output more easily understood by security engineers.
The PASTA methodology integrates financial reports with technical requirements, making the output more easily understood by upper management.
options_why: PASTA integrates the two. It does not separate them.
The result is made for upper management, not for engineers.
PASTA integrates business objectives, not financial reports.
cards.answer: The PASTA methodology integrates business objectives with technical requirements, making the output more easily understood by upper management.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: business objectives with technical requirements, so upper management understands.

cards.question: Say, from memory, the official sentence about what makes “PASTA” useful for management.
cards.answer: The PASTA methodology integrates business objectives with technical requirements, making the output more easily understood by upper management.
cards.explanation: Remember these parts: business objectives with technical requirements, so upper management understands.

cards.question: A team uses PASTA. Which step does it do FIRST?
options: Application decomposition
Threat analysis
Define objectives
Risk and impact analysis
options_why: This is step three. It needs the objectives and the scope first.
This is step four, after the application is split into parts.
This is the last step, step seven.
cards.answer: Define objectives
cards.explanation: PASTA starts from the goals of the business.

cards.question: Which PASTA step comes right AFTER application decomposition?
options: Threat analysis
Define technical scope
Vulnerability analysis
Attack enumeration
options_why: This comes before decomposition.
This comes after threat analysis.
This comes after vulnerability analysis.
cards.answer: Threat analysis
cards.explanation: When the application is split into parts, you look for threats on each part.

cards.question: Why is PASTA useful for management?
options: It replaces all technical work
It removes the need to list threats
It links business goals with technical needs
It sorts threats into six types
options_why: PASTA still needs technical work. It links that work to business goals.
PASTA has a step for threat analysis.
This is STRIDE, not PASTA.
cards.answer: It links business goals with technical needs
cards.explanation: The result starts from business objectives, so upper management can understand it.

cards.question: A security team gives management a long technical report. Management does not understand it. Which method would BEST help?
options: PASTA
STRIDE
A longer report with more technical details
The attacker-centric approach alone
options_why: STRIDE sorts threats into types. It does not link them to business goals.
More details would make the problem worse.
This approach profiles attackers. It does not link the work to business goals.
cards.answer: PASTA
cards.explanation: PASTA starts from business objectives, so its output is easier for management to understand.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a step of PASTA?
options: Application decomposition
Attack enumeration
Risk and impact analysis
Security awareness training
options_why: This is step three of PASTA.
This is step six of PASTA.
This is step seven of PASTA.
cards.answer: Security awareness training
cards.explanation: The seven steps of PASTA do not include training.

cards.question: A team wants to look for weak points straight away. According to PASTA, what should it do FIRST?
options: Define the technical scope
Define the business objectives
Split the application into parts
List the possible attacks
options_why: This is step two. The objectives come before it.
This is step three. Two steps come before it.
This is step six, near the end.
cards.answer: Define the business objectives
cards.explanation: The goal guides what deserves to be protected first.

cards.question: Which PASTA step is MOST concerned with the cost of an attack to the business?
options: Threat analysis
Risk and impact analysis
Define technical scope
Application decomposition
options_why: This step looks for the threats, not the cost.
This step marks the limits of the study.
This step splits the application into parts.
cards.answer: Risk and impact analysis
cards.explanation: You finish by measuring the risk and the impact of an attack.
